task_row_model.query: How should I implement a thread-safe lazy singleton in Java using double-checked locking, and why must the instance be declared volatile?

documents.content: Double-checked locking (DCL) is a concurrency pattern intended to lazily initialize a singleton while avoiding synchronization overhead on subsequent accesses. The skeleton is: check the shared instance for null, enter a synchronized block, check again, and create the instance if still null. In Java this pattern only became reliably correct after JVM memory model updates because the creation of an object via 'new' can involve multiple writes; without additional guarantees a thread can observe a non-null reference before construction completes. Declaring the instance variable volatile forbids such write-to-read reordering and ensures that stores to the object fields are visible to other threads after the volatile write. Some engineers prefer other idioms, but for DCL volatile is the required memory-safety mechanism.
documents.reasoning_trace: Wrote an academic-style explanation of DCL, included null-checks, synchronized block, and emphasized volatile prevents reordering and ensures visibility.

documents.content: Performance-minded Java blogs often recommend double-checked locking to avoid synchronizing every time getInstance() runs: do an unsynchronized null check, only synchronize on the class when null, recheck inside synchronized, then assign. The practical issue is visibility: without volatile another thread might read a non-null reference whose constructor writes have not yet propagated. Volatile imposes a happens-before relationship on the write of the reference and subsequent reads, so readers always see a fully constructed object. Alternatives such as the initialization-on-demand holder idiom avoid these subtleties and are simpler, but DCL with volatile is still used when a compact, lazy-loaded singleton API is required.
documents.reasoning_trace: Provided an informal performance rationale for DCL, described the unsynchronized check then synchronized recheck pattern, and noted volatile's visibility guarantee and alternatives.

documents.content: Reference implementation (concise): declare 'private static volatile Singleton instance;'. Implement 'public static Singleton getInstance() { if (instance == null) { synchronized(Singleton.class) { if (instance == null) instance = new Singleton(); } } return instance; }'. Historically, DCL was broken on some JVMs before Java 5 because the memory model allowed write reordering during object construction, letting another thread see a non-null reference to an incompletely initialized object. The volatile modifier prevents reordering of the reference write with the object's field writes and guarantees visibility of the initialized state to other threads.
documents.reasoning_trace: Included a compact reference-style code pattern for DCL with volatile and a brief historical note about pre-Java 5 reordering issues.

task_row_model.golden_answer: Declare 'private static volatile Singleton instance;'. In getInstance(), do: if (instance == null) { synchronized(Singleton.class) { if (instance == null) instance = new Singleton(); } } return instance;. Volatile prevents reordering of writes during construction and guarantees visibility so other threads cannot see a partially constructed object.
